posts.title: Anthropic's Model Hardware Standard: One Driver for Any Lab Instrument
posts.subtitle: An MCP-based protocol cuts lab-equipment integration from months to minutes
posts.summary: Anthropic's Model Hardware Standard (MHS) is a research-preview protocol that gives AI agents a universal, MCP-based way to drive lab and manufacturing hardware — collapsing custom integrations that used to take weeks into hours. Six early partners, including Genentech and QuEra Computing, report concrete speed and reliability gains, but MHS is still a limited preview, not an open standard yet.

slides.title: Robots and Instruments That Finally Speak One Language
slides.body: Anthropic introduced the Model Hardware Standard (MHS): a shared driver specification that lets AI agents safely operate real lab and manufacturing equipment, built on protocols including MCP.

slides.title: Every Instrument Speaks Its Own Dialect
slides.body: Integrating a new liquid handler, robotic arm, or microscope with orchestration software has traditionally taken weeks to months of specialist work.
bullets: Most lab and manufacturing devices have no shared interconnection protocol
Each device-plus-software pairing needs its own bespoke integration
That overhead is a big reason closed-loop, autonomous lab experiments stay rare

slides.title: A Standardized Driver, Not a New Protocol Per Device
slides.body: Anthropic describes MHS as 'a standardized driver: software that translates between a computer's operating system and a hardware device' — using simple primitives any device can expose.
bullets: Core primitives are just 'read' and 'write' commands any instrument can implement
Device discovery makes equipment findable on a network in a standard format
Natural-language tags let a technician describe a device in plain English, which the system turns into an operational reference file
Model-agnostic and built on protocols including MCP, so any MCP-capable agent can drive the hardware

slides.title: Six Early Partners, Concrete Results
slides.body: Anthropic tested MHS with six organizations before this preview.

rows: Automated BCA protein assays across liquid handlers, robotic arms, and plate readers
Unified microscopy rigs across seven incompatible vendor interfaces

slides.title: QuEra: From Manual Tuning to a 99.3% Success Rate
slides.body: QuEra Computing's quantum hardware depends on lasers staying precisely locked to a target frequency — previously a manual, error-prone tuning process.
bullets: Before MHS: ad hoc scripts per instrument, with laser-locking succeeding only about 58% of the time
With MHS: an agent reads live sensor state and writes correction commands through the same standardized driver interface used across every other device
Result: laser-locking success jumped to 99.3%, without QuEra writing a new bespoke integration for each laser controller

slides.title: Research Preview, Not a Public Standard Yet
slides.body: MHS is available to select scientific labs and manufacturers, not generally released.
bullets: Anthropic plans to open-source MHS only after completing safety evaluations and best-practice guidance
Safety stakes are higher than typical software: a bad write command can damage equipment or injure someone
Early integrators like AWS, Tecan, and Universal Robots are building support ahead of any public release
Not useful yet if you're not inside the preview — there's no public SDK or spec to adopt today

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: MHS is Anthropic betting that the bottleneck for autonomous science isn't model capability — it's the absence of a shared hardware interface.
bullets: A standardized read/write driver layer, discoverable on the network, built on protocols including MCP
Six partners already report multi-x speedups or reliability jumps (e.g. QuEra's 58% → 99.3% laser-locking)
Still a limited research preview — open-sourcing is gated on safety evaluation first
Worth tracking if you work anywhere AI agents need to touch physical lab or manufacturing hardware

questions.explanation: MHS is a standardized driver layer with simple read/write primitives, so an agent doesn't need a bespoke integration for every device, liquid handler, robotic arm, or microscope it touches.

posts.title: Grouped-Query Attention: The Middle Ground Between MHA and MQA
posts.subtitle: Why Llama 2, Mistral, and most production LLMs share key/value heads in groups
posts.summary: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) splits a transformer's query heads into groups that each share one key/value head, sitting between full multi-head attention and multi-query attention. It shrinks the KV cache by the group-size factor while staying much closer to full-MHA quality than MQA, which is why Llama 2 70B and Mistral both ship with it by default.

slides.title: One Set of Keys and Values, Shared by a Group of Query Heads
slides.body: Multi-head attention gives every head its own key/value projection. Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) splits heads into groups that share one K/V projection per group — cutting KV-cache memory without multi-query attention's quality hit.

slides.title: Multi-Head Attention's KV Cache Doesn't Scale
slides.body: Each of a model's attention heads keeps its own cached key and value vectors for every previous token.
bullets: KV-cache size scales with the number of heads, not just the model's parameter count
At long context lengths, the KV cache can rival or exceed the model weights in memory footprint
Multi-Query Attention (MQA) fixes this by sharing just one key/value head across all queries — but measurably hurts output quality versus full MHA

slides.title: Split Heads Into Groups, Share Within Each Group
slides.body: GQA (Ainslie et al., 2023) groups a model's H query heads into G groups, where each group shares a single key/value head.
bullets: G = H recovers standard multi-head attention exactly; G = 1 recovers MQA exactly — GQA is the general form in between
A common setting: 32 query heads grouped into 8 KV heads, so 4 queries share each KV head
KV-cache size shrinks by the grouping factor (H / G) versus full MHA, with no change to the query-side computation

slides.title: Three Points on the Same Spectrum
slides.body: GQA isn't a separate idea from MHA and MQA — it's the tunable middle ground between them.

slides.title: Llama 2 70B's Real Numbers
slides.body: Llama 2's larger models are the textbook production example of GQA.
bullets: Llama 2 34B and 70B use 8 KV-head groups shared across their query heads — an 8x reduction in cached K/V tensors per layer versus full MHA
Mistral 7B also ships GQA by default, which helps keep its sliding-window attention cheap over long contexts
The smaller Llama 2 models (7B, 13B) kept full MHA, since their KV cache was never big enough to be the bottleneck

slides.title: Not Free: a Fixed Architecture Choice
slides.body: GQA is a design decision baked in before training, not a runtime switch.
bullets: The group count is fixed at pretraining time; changing it later needs a conversion or distillation step, not just a config flag
Fewer KV heads means less per-head specialization in what gets cached — a real, if usually small, capacity cost
Skip it for small models or short-context use cases where the KV cache was never the memory bottleneck in the first place

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: GQA is the practical default for large, long-context LLMs because it buys most of MQA's memory savings while keeping almost all of MHA's quality.
bullets: G = H is MHA, G = 1 is MQA — GQA is the tunable spectrum between them
KV-cache size shrinks by H / G, directly cutting memory and speeding up decoding at long context
Llama 2 70B: 8 KV-head groups; Mistral 7B: GQA by default
A pretraining-time architecture choice, not something you toggle after the fact

questions.prompt: In Grouped-Query Attention, what happens when the number of groups G equals the number of query heads H?
options: It becomes multi-query attention (MQA)
It becomes standard multi-head attention (MHA)
The model stops using a KV cache entirely
It triggers sliding-window attention
questions.explanation: When G = H, every query head gets its own key/value head — exactly standard multi-head attention. GQA's groups are what let you dial between MHA (G=H) and MQA (G=1).

questions.prompt: Why does GQA typically stay closer to full MHA quality than MQA does?
options: It uses a larger vocabulary size
It only shares KV heads within small groups rather than collapsing all heads to a single shared KV head
It adds an extra attention layer
It increases the number of query heads
questions.explanation: MQA forces every query head to share one single KV head, a large reduction in representational diversity. GQA only shares within smaller groups, preserving more of the per-head specialization that MHA has.

questions.prompt: How many KV-head groups does Llama 2 70B use for its query heads?
options: 1 (full MQA)
64 (full MHA, no sharing)
8 KV-head groups
It doesn't use GQA at all
questions.explanation: Llama 2's 34B and 70B models use 8 KV-head groups, giving an 8x reduction in cached key/value tensors per layer compared to full multi-head attention.

references.title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints (arXiv:2305.13245)

posts.title: LoopCD: Free Accuracy From a Model's Own Earlier Guess
posts.subtitle: Apple researchers mine signal looped transformers were throwing away at every step
posts.summary: LoopCD is a training-free decoding trick for looped transformers: contrast the final recurrent pass against an earlier one to pick better tokens. It lifts AIME 2024 pass@1 on Ouro-2.6B-Thinking from 61.88% to 73.33%, and lets models halve their loop count while matching full-depth accuracy, cutting FLOPs 22.5%-48.2%.

slides.title: A Model Already Knows More Than It Tells You
slides.body: Looped transformers reuse one block across several recurrent passes to act deeper without adding parameters. Apple's LoopCD shows each pass's intermediate guess carries real signal — and you can mine it for free at decode time.

slides.title: Every Loop But the Last Gets Thrown Away
slides.body: Looping a shared block N times gives a model the effective capacity of an N-times-deeper network, and each loop's hidden state is already decodable into a plausible next token.
bullets: Standard decoding reads only the final loop and discards every earlier one
More loops improves reasoning but costs proportionally more FLOPs per generated token
No existing training-free method used the discarded intermediate passes as a signal

slides.title: Contrast the Final Pass Against an Earlier One
slides.body: LoopCD is a training-free contrastive decoding framework: it boosts tokens where more recurrent computation actually changed the model's mind, instead of penalizing tokens the model already favored early.
bullets: No new weights, no fine-tuning — applied purely at decode time on an existing looped model
Works on any model that already loops a shared block, e.g. Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, Huginn

slides.title: Two Flavors: Logit-Space or Hidden-Space
slides.body: LoopCD comes in two variants depending on where the contrast happens.
bullets: LoopCD-Logits: runs one extra output pass and contrasts final vs. earlier logits directly
LoopCD-Hidden: contrasts hidden states before the unembedding layer — zero extra output-head passes
Hidden-space is cheaper per step; logit-space needs raw access to an earlier loop's full distribution

slides.title: Same Weights, Measurably Better Answers
slides.body: Both variants produce large, consistent gains at full recurrent depth on their respective benchmarks.

slides.title: Halving the Loop Budget on a Math Benchmark
slides.body: Say Ouro-2.6B-Thinking normally runs 8 recurrent loops per token to hit its best AIME score. The paper shows that with LoopCD's contrastive guidance, running only 4 loops can still match or beat the unguided 8-loop baseline.
bullets: That halves per-token compute while holding accuracy steady
Measured FLOPs reduction across settings: 22.5% to 48.2% versus the full-depth unguided baseline

slides.title: Where the Free Lunch Runs Out
slides.body: LoopCD isn't strictly free in every setting.
bullets: LoopCD-Logits adds a real extra forward pass through the output head — costly with large vocabularies
LoopCD-Hidden needs raw hidden-state access, which closed, API-only models don't expose
If early and final loops are confidently wrong in the same direction, there's no useful contrast signal to amplify

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: LoopCD turns a looped transformer's own discarded intermediate guesses into a free accuracy or efficiency win — no retraining required.
bullets: Contrast final-loop vs. earlier-loop predictions instead of decoding only the last one
LoopCD-Logits: more accurate, costs one extra output pass
LoopCD-Hidden: zero extra output overhead, needs internal access
Net effect: halve loop count at matched accuracy, or keep full depth for a real accuracy jump

questions.prompt: What does LoopCD contrast to decide the next token at decode time?
options: The final-loop prediction against a human-written reference answer
The final-loop prediction against one of the model's own earlier recurrent-loop predictions
Two entirely different models' predictions
The current token embedding against the previous token embedding
questions.explanation: LoopCD is self-contrastive: it compares the model's final-loop output against an earlier loop's output from the same forward pass, amplifying directions where extra computation actually changed the answer.

questions.prompt: On the HumanEval benchmark, LoopCD-Hidden lifted Huginn's pass@1 from what baseline to what result?
options: 19,400 to 52,000 tokens/sec
20% to 40% utilization
questions.explanation: LoopCD-Hidden raised Huginn's HumanEval pass@1 from 22.56% to 31.71%. The 61.88%-to-73.33% jump is a different result: Ouro-2.6B-Thinking's AIME 2024 pass@1 under LoopCD-Logits.

questions.prompt: Why can LoopCD-Logits add more latency than LoopCD-Hidden, even though both are training-free?
options: LoopCD-Logits requires retraining the unembedding layer first
LoopCD-Logits needs an extra forward pass through the output head to get a second logit distribution
LoopCD-Logits only works on models with fewer than 1B parameters
LoopCD-Logits doubles the total number of recurrent loops
questions.explanation: Contrasting in logit space means projecting through the vocabulary head an extra time, which is real added compute on large vocabularies. LoopCD-Hidden contrasts earlier, on hidden states, so it skips that extra output-head pass entirely.

references.title: Decoding Looped Transformers Better for (Almost) Free (arXiv:2610.02185)

posts.title: Ai2 Open-Sources the Training Stack Behind Trillion-Parameter MoEs
posts.subtitle: Olmo-Core 3 brings documented, reproducible benchmarks to a scale only closed labs used to report
posts.summary: The Allen Institute for AI released Olmo-Core 3, a redesigned open training framework for large mixture-of-experts models, benchmarked past 1 trillion total parameters. On a 47B-parameter MoE across 8 NVIDIA B300 GPUs it hit 2.7x the throughput of the prior FSDP-based stack, and it scaled experts 8-to-128 while active parameters and training speed barely moved.

slides.title: The Infra Behind Giant MoEs Is Usually a Trade Secret
slides.body: Frontier labs train multi-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts models, but the training stacks that make it work rarely get published in enough detail to reproduce.

slides.title: Open MoE Training Lags at the Scales That Matter
slides.body: Open training frameworks exist, but most haven't published fully documented benchmarks past the trillion-parameter mark, where real bottlenecks like all-to-all expert communication and memory fragmentation actually bite.
bullets: Below that scale, inefficiencies in routing and memory layout are easy to miss
Without reproducible numbers, researchers can't tell which training-stack decisions actually matter at frontier scale

slides.title: Olmo-Core 3: Redesigned, Open, and Benchmarked Past 1T Parameters
slides.body: Olmo-Core 3 is Ai2's rebuilt open training framework for mixture-of-experts language models, released October 1, 2026, and already serving as the infrastructure layer under Ai2's next-generation Olmo models.
bullets: Fully open source, built and benchmarked on NVIDIA B300 GPUs
Publishes configs and numbers at scales most labs only discuss internally

slides.title: 2.7x the Throughput, Same GPUs
slides.body: In a preliminary test, a 47-billion-parameter MoE on 8 NVIDIA B300 GPUs moved from the older FSDP-based implementation to the new stack.

slides.title: Growing Experts Without Breaking the Budget
slides.body: Ai2 also tested scaling the expert pool from 8 to 128 while keeping 4 experts active per token.
bullets: Active parameters stayed roughly fixed at ~3.2B even as total capacity grew from 4.6B to 47B
Training throughput fell by less than 5% despite that 16x jump in total parameters

Separately, switching to MXFP8 precision (vs. BF16) on 4 B300 GPUs gave ~21% higher throughput, with peak active memory falling from 103GiB to 95GiB — most of the gain came from feed-forward compute and inter-expert data movement

slides.title: Stress-Testing at 1.2 Trillion Parameters
slides.body: Ai2 pushed Olmo-Core 3 to a 1.2-trillion-parameter configuration with 58.36 billion active parameters per token, spread across 512 GPUs — a scale and level of detail previously reported mostly by closed labs.
bullets: This is the regime where routing imbalance and communication overhead usually show up first
Publishing numbers here, not just at toy scale, is what makes the benchmark actually useful to other teams

slides.title: What This Release Doesn't Hand You
slides.body: Olmo-Core 3 is training infrastructure and benchmarks, not a ready-to-use frontier model.
bullets: The throughput numbers come from Ai2's own B300 clusters on preliminary tests — your mileage depends on interconnect and cluster topology
The MXFP8 gains assume load is distributed uniformly across experts, which real production traffic rarely guarantees
You still need to pretrain a model on top of this stack to get anything deployable

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Olmo-Core 3 closes some of the gap between what closed labs can do at trillion-parameter MoE scale and what the open community can reproduce.
bullets: 2.7x throughput gain on a 47B MoE by replacing an older FSDP-based stack
Experts scaled 8→128 with active params and speed almost unchanged
MXFP8 precision adds ~21% more throughput on top
Benchmarked up to 1.2T total parameters across 512 GPUs, fully documented

questions.prompt: What throughput improvement did Ai2 measure for Olmo-Core 3 on a 47B-parameter MoE across 8 NVIDIA B300 GPUs, versus the older FSDP-based stack?
options: About 1.2x
About 2.7x — from roughly 19,400 to 52,000 tokens/sec per GPU
About 10x
No throughput change, only a memory improvement
questions.explanation: Ai2 reported roughly 19,400 tokens/sec/GPU on the prior FSDP-based implementation versus roughly 52,000 on Olmo-Core 3 — about 2.7x.

questions.prompt: When Ai2 scaled the expert pool from 8 to 128 while keeping 4 experts active per token, what happened?
options: Active parameters exploded to 47B and throughput collapsed
Active parameters stayed roughly fixed (~3.2B) and training throughput fell less than 5%
The model stopped converging entirely
Throughput doubled along with active parameters
questions.explanation: Because only 4 experts are active per token regardless of pool size, active parameters stayed near 3.2B even as total capacity grew 4.6B→47B, and throughput dropped less than 5%.

questions.prompt: What mainly drove the ~21% throughput gain Ai2 measured when switching to MXFP8 precision?
options: Using a newer, faster GPU model
Gains mostly from feed-forward computation and data movement between experts
Removing the output/unembedding layer
Switching from a mixture-of-experts to a dense architecture
questions.explanation: Ai2 attributed most of the MXFP8-vs-BF16 gain to faster feed-forward computation and inter-expert data movement, alongside peak active memory dropping from 103GiB to 95GiB.

posts.title: PagedAttention: Virtual Memory for the KV Cache
posts.subtitle: How vLLM stopped LLM serving from wasting most of its own GPU memory
posts.summary: PagedAttention splits each request's KV cache into non-contiguous, fixed-size blocks managed by a block table, borrowing the OS idea of virtual memory paging. It cut KV-cache memory waste from 60-80% to under 4% and let vLLM serve 2-4x higher throughput than prior systems at the same latency.

slides.title: The Cache That Ate the GPU
slides.body: Before vLLM, serving an LLM meant reserving a worst-case chunk of memory for every request's attention cache — and most of that memory sat empty.

slides.title: Reserving for the Worst Case Wastes Almost Everything
slides.body: Each request's key/value cache was allocated as one contiguous block sized for the maximum possible sequence length, because attention needs contiguous memory to read efficiently.
bullets: Most requests finish far short of the max length, so most of the reserved block goes unused
Fixed contiguous blocks fragment GPU memory between requests of different sizes
Pre-vLLM systems like Orca used only about 20-40% of reserved KV-cache memory for actual live tokens

slides.title: Borrow the OS Trick: Pages, Not One Big Block
slides.body: PagedAttention splits each sequence's KV cache into fixed-size blocks that don't need to sit contiguously in GPU memory, tracked with a per-sequence block table — the same idea operating systems use for virtual memory paging.
bullets: A new block is only allocated once a sequence actually grows into it
The attention kernel reads through the block table instead of assuming one flat buffer

slides.title: Sharing Pages Between Requests
slides.body: Decoupling logical tokens from physical memory location means multiple sequences can point at the same physical blocks.
bullets: Parallel sampling or beam search can share a common prompt prefix's pages instead of copying them
Copy-on-write kicks in only when one branch actually diverges from a shared prefix
Shared prefixes cost close to zero extra memory instead of one full copy per branch

slides.title: What Paging Actually Bought
slides.body: The original vLLM paper reports the following at matched latency.

slides.title: 100 Chat Sessions, Wildly Different Lengths
slides.body: Picture a server handling 100 concurrent chats: some users send one short line, others paste a 4,000-token document. A pre-paging system reserves max-length space for all 100 up front, so most of that memory sits idle on the short chats.
bullets: PagedAttention grows each sequence's pages only as it actually generates tokens
The memory freed by short sequences lets far more requests fit in the same GPU, raising batch size and throughput together

slides.title: Paging Isn't Entirely Free
slides.body: Non-contiguous memory access through a block table adds real bookkeeping compared to one flat buffer.
bullets: Block-table lookups add small per-step kernel overhead versus a single contiguous read
Too small a block size means more table entries and overhead; too large brings back fragmentation at the tail of each sequence
If your workload is already uniform, fixed-length batches, the win shrinks — there's little fragmentation to recover

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: PagedAttention treats the KV cache like paged virtual memory instead of one worst-case contiguous block.
bullets: Memory waste: 60-80% before, under 4% after
Enables near-free sharing of common prefixes across parallel samples or beam search branches
2-4x throughput at the same latency versus FasterTransformer and Orca
Tradeoff: small per-step bookkeeping cost and a block-size tuning decision

questions.prompt: What was the main cause of GPU memory waste in LLM serving systems before PagedAttention?
options: Models were too large to fit on a single GPU
Each request reserved one contiguous, worst-case-sized block of KV-cache memory regardless of actual sequence length
The attention math itself was numerically unstable
GPUs of that era didn't have enough compute cores
questions.explanation: Because attention needed one contiguous buffer, systems reserved space for the maximum possible sequence length per request — and most requests never used most of it.

questions.prompt: How does PagedAttention let parallel samples that share the same prompt save memory?
options: It deletes the prompt from memory after the first sample finishes
It compresses the KV cache with quantization
It lets sequences share the same physical blocks for a common prefix, copying only when a branch diverges
It writes the shared prompt's cache to disk and reloads it per sample
questions.explanation: Because logical tokens are mapped to physical blocks through a table, multiple sequences can point at the same physical pages for a shared prefix, with copy-on-write only when one branch actually changes.

questions.prompt: What's a genuine cost of adopting PagedAttention-style memory management?
options: It only runs on CPUs, not GPUs
Block-table-based, non-contiguous access adds small per-step bookkeeping overhead versus one flat buffer
It requires retraining the model from scratch
It caps maximum context length at 512 tokens
questions.explanation: Reading through a block table instead of one flat buffer adds real, if small, per-step overhead, and picking a good block size is itself a tuning tradeoff between table overhead and tail fragmentation.

references.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention (arXiv:2309.06180)

posts.title: The Sharpening Tax: What RL Post-Training Quietly Costs You
posts.subtitle: Base models beat their fine-tuned successors when given enough tries — here's the metric that proves it
posts.summary: A new Meta Superintelligence Labs study shows RL post-training boosts single-shot accuracy by narrowing a model's solution diversity — a cost the authors call the 'sharpening tax.' Across 42 model-benchmark pairs, base models with a simple inference harness often out-sample their post-trained versions given enough attempts. Their fix, PTGS, tempers sampling per-prompt to cut the tax without giving up accuracy.

slides.title: RL Post-Training Has a Hidden Tax
slides.body: Post-training makes a model more likely to nail its best-guess answer on the first try. The price: it quietly becomes less likely to find the right answer any other way.
bullets: Meta Superintelligence Labs + UW-Madison, NYU, Stanford
42 model-benchmark cases, 128 rollouts per task

slides.title: Pass@1 Goes Up. Pass@K Can Go Down.
slides.body: Leaderboards report pass@1 — accuracy on a single sampled attempt. But real agent harnesses retry, branch, and self-correct, so what matters is pass@K: do ANY of K attempts succeed?
bullets: Base models + a light inference harness often beat their RL-tuned siblings on pass@K
This holds despite the base model having much lower pass@1
Tested on 14 open base/post-trained checkpoint pairs across 4 model families

slides.title: Why: RL Collapses Probability Mass
slides.body: RL post-training reinforces whichever trajectory already worked during training, pushing sampling probability onto a narrow set of outputs. One path gets sharper; the others get starved.
bullets: Base model: samples spread across many plausible strategies → more coverage at high K
Post-trained model: samples cluster tightly around one learned strategy → less coverage if that strategy is wrong for this prompt
The authors name this gap the 'Sharpening Tax' and define two variants, tax_A and tax_S, to measure it

slides.title: The Tax, Measured
slides.body: Benchmarks: BFCL v4 multi-turn, WebShop, and ACEBench — all agentic, multi-step tasks where an agent's harness can retry.

rows: Broad coverage; many paths to a correct answer
Keeps the accuracy gain, keeps more coverage

slides.title: A WebShop Agent, Two Ways
slides.body: WebShop drops an agent into a shopping site and gives it a buyer instruction (e.g. 'find a size-8 waterproof hiking boot under $90').
bullets: Base model: samples 8 different search-and-filter strategies; 3 of them independently land on a correct product page
RL-tuned model: samples 8 times but all 8 follow the one filtering pattern it was rewarded for during training — if that pattern misses this product catalog's layout, all 8 fail
Give the harness a retry budget (K>1) and the base model's diversity starts winning

slides.title: The Fix: Posterior-Tempered Group Sampling (PTGS)
slides.body: Instead of one fixed sampling temperature for every prompt, PTGS estimates each prompt's difficulty from a Bayesian posterior and sets the rollout temperature per-prompt.
bullets: Easy prompts → lower temperature, sharpen freely (little coverage to lose)
Hard prompts → higher temperature, preserve exploration during RL training itself
Result: pays a smaller sharpening tax than a fixed-temperature baseline while still improving pass@1

slides.title: When the Tax Doesn't Matter
slides.body: If your product only ever gets one shot — a single customer-facing chat reply with no retry loop — pass@1 is the number that matters, and standard RL post-training is still the right call.
bullets: Tax matters most for agent harnesses with retries, tool-use loops, or best-of-N sampling
Tax matters less for single-shot, low-latency, no-retry deployments
A model can look 'worse' on a leaderboard (lower pass@1) and still be the better agent backbone

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: RL post-training trades solution breadth for single-shot sharpness — that trade is a real, measurable 'tax'
Base models with a simple harness can out-perform post-trained models at pass@K despite much lower pass@1
Measure pass@K, not just pass@1, if your agent gets more than one attempt
PTGS tempers sampling per-prompt by difficulty, cutting the tax without giving back the accuracy gain

questions.prompt: What does the 'Sharpening Tax' measure?
options: How much GPU memory RL post-training consumes
The loss in test-time scalability (pass@K coverage) that RL post-training causes while raising pass@1
The dollar cost of running RLHF versus pretraining
The latency added by a retry loop
questions.explanation: The tax quantifies how much solution coverage (pass@K) a model loses as a side-effect of RL post-training sharpening its pass@1 accuracy.

questions.prompt: Why can a base model beat its RL-tuned version at pass@K despite a lower pass@1?
options: Base models are larger
RL post-training corrupts the model's weights
RL post-training narrows sampling onto one learned strategy, while the base model's samples stay spread across many strategies
Pass@K is not a valid metric
questions.explanation: Post-training reinforces the trajectory that worked during training, concentrating probability mass there — which helps pass@1 but hurts the diversity that pass@K rewards.

questions.prompt: How does PTGS reduce the sharpening tax?
options: By training on more data
By using a single fixed low temperature for every prompt
By setting each prompt's rollout temperature from a Bayesian estimate of that prompt's difficulty
By disabling RL post-training entirely
questions.explanation: PTGS (posterior-tempered group sampling) adapts sampling temperature per-prompt based on a Bayesian difficulty estimate, preserving exploration on hard prompts while still sharpening easy ones.

posts.title: HNSW: Why Vector Search Doesn't Scan Everything
posts.subtitle: The graph structure behind sub-millisecond nearest-neighbor search in every vector database you use
posts.summary: Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs are the default index behind FAISS, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, and Milvus. Instead of comparing a query to every stored vector, HNSW builds a multi-layer graph that lets search 'zoom in' from a sparse top layer to a dense bottom layer in roughly logarithmic time — trading a small amount of recall for a massive speedup.

slides.title: A Graph, Not a Scan
slides.body: Brute-force nearest-neighbor search compares your query vector to every vector in the database. HNSW instead walks a graph, checking a tiny fraction of the vectors to find an excellent approximate answer.

slides.title: Brute Force Doesn't Scale
slides.body: Exact k-nearest-neighbor search is O(n) per query — compare against every stored vector.
bullets: 10K vectors: brute force is fine, often faster than building an index
10M+ vectors: brute force means scanning millions of floating-point comparisons on every single query
A RAG pipeline that calls this per user turn needs query latency in milliseconds, not seconds

slides.title: Layers, Sparse to Dense
slides.body: HNSW builds several stacked graph layers. The top layer has very few nodes with long-range links; each layer below adds more nodes with shorter, denser links, until the bottom layer holds every vector.
bullets: Search starts at a single entry point in the sparsest top layer
At each layer, it greedily hops to the neighbor closest to the query until no neighbor improves — then drops down a layer
By the time it reaches the bottom layer, it's already near the true answer and only needs to refine locally

slides.title: Walking the Graph
slides.body: Query: find vectors near embedding Q in a 10-million-vector index with 4 layers.
bullets: Layer 3 (sparsest, ~hundreds of nodes): jump from the entry point toward Q, land near the right neighborhood in a handful of hops
Layer 2 → Layer 1: descend, each layer narrowing the search to a tighter local region around Q
Layer 0 (every vector): explore ef_search candidate neighbors in that local region and return the top-k closest
Total comparisons: a few hundred, not 10 million

slides.title: HNSW vs. the Alternatives

rows: Highest — stores graph edges per node
Inserts are OK; deletes are awkward

slides.title: Tradeoffs and Pitfalls
bullets: Memory overhead: each vector stores M graph edges per layer (M typically 16–64) — on top of the raw vector, that adds up fast at hundreds of millions of vectors
Approximate, not exact: HNSW can miss the true nearest neighbor; tune ef_search up for more recall at the cost of latency
Deletes are expensive: removing a node means patching the graph edges that pointed to it, so most engines mark-and-rebuild instead of deleting live
Skip it for small collections (under ~10K vectors) — brute force is simpler and often just as fast there
Skip it when you need guaranteed-exact results, e.g. deduplication against a known exact match

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: HNSW trades a small amount of recall for roughly logarithmic query time versus linear brute force
It works by searching sparse-to-dense graph layers, narrowing in on the answer before touching the full dataset
Tune M and ef_construction at build time, ef_search at query time — more of either means higher recall, more latency
It's the default choice for large, mostly-read vector workloads; reconsider it for tiny datasets or heavy-delete workloads

questions.prompt: Why is HNSW faster than brute-force nearest-neighbor search?
options: It stores vectors in a compressed format
It only searches a random sample of vectors
It walks a multi-layer graph from sparse to dense, comparing against a small fraction of vectors instead of all of them
It uses a GPU instead of a CPU
questions.explanation: HNSW narrows down the search region layer by layer before doing a small local search at the bottom layer, avoiding a full linear scan.

questions.prompt: What's the main cost of using HNSW instead of a flat index?
options: It requires a GPU
It is always slower than brute force
It only works with text data
It uses more memory (graph edges per node) and returns approximate, not exact, results
questions.explanation: HNSW stores extra graph edges per vector and trades exactness for speed — typically 95-99% recall depending on tuning.

questions.prompt: When should you reach for brute-force (flat) search instead of HNSW?
options: When you have billions of vectors
When you need guaranteed-exact results or your collection is small (e.g. under ~10K vectors)
When query latency doesn't matter at all and recall must be approximate
Never — HNSW is always better
questions.explanation: At small scale, brute force is simple and fast enough; and when exactness is required (e.g. dedup), an approximate index like HNSW is the wrong tool.

posts.title: Quine: Microsoft's World Model for Biology
posts.subtitle: One weekend to go from thousands of compounds to a wet-lab shortlist
posts.summary: Microsoft Research introduced Quine, a multimodal world model spanning five biological domains, paired with an interactive harness of tools and literature. In a Broad Institute collaboration on pancreatic cancer, it narrowed thousands of candidate compounds to a validated shortlist in a single weekend.

slides.title: Biology Doesn't Fit in One Model
slides.body: Microsoft Research's Quine is an early-stage world model trained jointly across five biological domains, built to let evidence in one modality inform predictions in another.
bullets: Announced Sept 29, 2026 by Nicolo Fusi & Jonathan M. Carlson
Built with the Broad Institute of Harvard and MIT
First public test: pancreatic cancer drug discovery

slides.title: Five Modalities, Usually Five Separate Models
slides.body: Genomics, protein structure, chemistry, RNA/cellular state, and bioimaging are each studied with their own specialized tools. A researcher connecting insight across all five has to do that synthesis by hand.
bullets: Hypothesis space is too large for intuition alone to search
Cross-modality reasoning (e.g. a genomic signal implying a chemical intervention) is slow and manual
Most AI-for-bio models are single-modality specialists

slides.title: A Joint World Model Plus a Research Harness
slides.body: Quine pairs a multimodal world model with an interactive harness that wires the model into orchestration systems, scientific tools, literature, and the researchers themselves.
bullets: World model trains jointly across genomics, protein structure/function, chemistry, RNA/cell state, and bioimaging
Harness lets the model call tools and pull in literature mid-reasoning, not just answer from static weights
Goal: computationally search a hypothesis space far larger than intuition allows, before anything touches a lab bench

slides.title: Case Study: Pancreatic Cancer Compound Screening
slides.body: Working with Broad Institute researchers, Quine was pointed at pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and asked to find compounds that could drive therapeutic tumor cell-state transitions.
bullets: Thousands of candidate compounds predicted and prioritized computationally
Search space narrowed to a handful of candidates for lab validation in one weekend
Top-ranked compounds produced the largest intended transcriptional shifts in the actual wet-lab assays

slides.title: One Model, Five Domains
slides.body: Most biological foundation models specialize in a single data type. Quine's bet is that joint training across modalities lets evidence compound instead of staying siloed.

rows: None — needs a human to connect findings
Built in — one model reasons across all five

slides.title: Research-Only, Not a Clinical Tool
slides.body: Microsoft is explicit about Quine's current limits: it's experimental, hypothesis-generation technology, not a diagnostic or treatment tool.
bullets: Microsoft's own disclaimer: 'intended only for research, not clinical or medical use'
Outputs 'may be incomplete or inaccurate' and require expert review plus real experimental validation
Access is currently limited to a 'Quine Fellows' cohort of selected scientists, not a public API
Takeaway: it compresses the hypothesis-generation step (weekend, not weeks) — it doesn't replace the wet lab

posts.title: ReAct: Reasoning and Acting, One Step at a Time
posts.subtitle: Why grounding each thought in a real observation beats reasoning in the dark
posts.summary: ReAct interleaves verbal reasoning ('Thought') with tool calls ('Action') and real results ('Observation') in a loop, so each reasoning step is grounded in fresh evidence instead of the model's own unchecked guesses. It's the pattern underneath most modern tool-using agents.

slides.title: Thought, Action, Observation — Repeat
slides.body: ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) interleaves reasoning traces with actions in the same loop, so a language model's next thought is conditioned on what actually happened, not just what it assumed.
bullets: Introduced in 'ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models'
Now the backbone pattern of most tool-calling LLM agents

slides.title: Pure Reasoning Hallucinates. Pure Acting Is Brittle.
slides.body: Chain-of-thought prompting lets a model reason step by step, but every step comes from its own parameters — a wrong 'fact' early on quietly corrupts everything after it. Action-only agents skip reasoning and just emit the next tool call, with no explicit place to notice when a plan has gone wrong.
bullets: Chain-of-thought alone: no mechanism to check a claim against the real world mid-reasoning
Act-only agents: no visible plan, so recovering from a bad action is hard
Both struggle on tasks that need multiple real-world lookups before answering

slides.title: Close the Loop: Thought → Action → Observation
slides.body: At each step the model writes a short Thought (what it currently believes and what it needs to find out), emits an Action (a tool call — search, calculator, API), and receives an Observation (the tool's real output). The next Thought is conditioned on that Observation.
bullets: Thought = plan/update reasoning in natural language
Action = a concrete, parsable tool call
Observation = ground truth fed back into context
Loop repeats until the model emits a final answer

slides.title: Worked Example: A Multi-Hop Question
slides.body: Question: 'Which of these two products launched first, and by how many years?' A ReAct agent doesn't guess — it looks each fact up before comparing.
bullets: Thought: I need the launch year of Product A. Action: search('Product A launch date'). Observation: 2019.
Thought: Now I need Product B's launch year. Action: search('Product B launch date'). Observation: 2022.
Thought: 2019 is earlier than 2022, difference is 3 years. Action: finish('Product A launched first, 3 years earlier').

slides.title: ReAct vs. the Two Pure Strategies
slides.body: The original paper found ReAct's interleaving reduces the hallucinated, uncorrectable reasoning chains seen with pure chain-of-thought, and improves task success over act-only agents on interactive benchmarks like ALFWorld and WebShop by giving the model a place to plan and recover.

rows: Yes, but can't self-correct against reality
Yes — acts on the real environment
No — no visible reasoning to debug
Yes — every thought follows a real observation

slides.title: When NOT to Reach for ReAct
slides.body: The Thought steps cost extra tokens and latency on every single turn — that's a real tradeoff, not a free upgrade.
bullets: Simple, single-step tasks (one lookup, no comparison) don't need a reasoning trace at all
If tools are unreliable or missing, ReAct still hallucinates — it can only ground on observations it actually receives
Without a clear stopping condition, the loop can wander — cap max steps and give the model a way to say 'I don't know'
Verbose thoughts aren't free: they add cost and latency on every single turn

slides.title: The Pattern Under Most Agent Frameworks
bullets: ReAct = Thought → Action → Observation, looped until a final answer
Grounding each reasoning step in a real tool result is what curbs hallucination
It trades extra tokens/latency for better recoverability on multi-step, tool-using tasks
Most production agent loops (ReAct-style prompting, function-calling agents) descend directly from this pattern

questions.prompt: What are the three steps in the ReAct loop?
options: Plan, Execute, Review
Thought, Action, Observation
Input, Process, Output
Reason, Retrieve, Rank
questions.explanation: ReAct interleaves a Thought (reasoning), an Action (tool call), and an Observation (real result), then loops — each new Thought is conditioned on the latest Observation.

questions.prompt: Why does interleaving actions with reasoning reduce hallucination compared to pure chain-of-thought?
options: It uses a bigger model
Each reasoning step gets grounded against a real observation instead of relying only on the model's own assumptions
It skips reasoning entirely
It only works with code-generation tasks
questions.explanation: Pure chain-of-thought reasons entirely from the model's parameters with no check against reality. ReAct forces a real-world observation after every action, so wrong assumptions get corrected before they compound.

questions.prompt: When is ReAct's extra reasoning overhead NOT worth it?
options: On any multi-step research task
On simple, single-step lookups where there's nothing to plan or recover from
Whenever tools are available
Only on coding tasks
questions.explanation: Thought steps cost tokens and latency on every turn. For a simple one-shot lookup with no comparison or recovery needed, that overhead buys nothing.

posts.title: AEWM: Editing an Agent's Reasoning Before It Goes Wrong
posts.subtitle: A world model that predicts how an agent's own next move will hurt its task, then rewrites that move before it executes.
posts.summary: AEWM (arXiv:2609.28416, RUC AI Box) targets "task-state contamination": the slow rot where a long-horizon agent's unsupported assumptions become accepted facts and partial progress gets mistaken for completion. Its Action Judge classifies each proposed step as Critical, Exploratory, or Noisy; noisy steps get rewritten by State Revision before they ever execute. Wired into real agent loops via EditAct, it lifts six-benchmark average scores by 3.2-6.7 points across three backbones.

bullets: Paper: "Agent-Editing World Model: Rethinking World Modeling for LLM Agents" (arXiv:2609.28416)
From RUC AI Box (Renmin University of China); code and benchmark released under Apache-2.0
Evaluated across 6 benchmarks and 3 agent backbones, including Search, Terminal, and SWE tasks
slides.title: A World Model That Edits the Agent, Not the Environment

slides.body: Most "world models" for agents try to predict what the environment will show next — the next tool output, the next screen. AEWM's authors point at a different failure mode: task-state contamination, where an agent's own reasoning corrupts its sense of what's true.
bullets: An unsupported assumption made early gets treated as settled fact for the rest of the run
Plans don't get revised even when later evidence contradicts them
Partial progress gets reported — and believed — as if the task were finished
slides.title: Long agent runs quietly rot from the inside

slides.body: AEWM predicts how the agent's own upcoming reasoning-and-action step will affect task progress, not what the environment will do. Action Judge scores that step; if it looks harmful, State Revision rewrites it before it ever runs.
bullets: Action Judge classifies each proposed step as Critical, Exploratory, or Noisy
Noisy steps are rewritten by State Revision before execution, not patched after the fact
EditAct loop: Propose → Judge → Edit → Act → Log, wired into real environment interaction
slides.title: Judge the next step before it executes, then edit it if it's bad

slides.body: On a held-out set of 3,000 agent decisions, Action Judge's classification is the load-bearing signal — and it pays off downstream once EditAct acts on it during real task execution.
slides.title: Catching bad decisions early compounds into real task gains

slides.body: A coding agent fixes a failing test, but its next tool call accidentally reruns a stale cached result that still shows green. The agent's following reasoning step is about to declare the task complete. Action Judge flags that step Noisy — the claim doesn't follow from a real passing run — and State Revision rewrites the reasoning to re-verify against a fresh test execution before any completion claim is made.
bullets: The bad step is caught at proposal time, before "task complete" is ever logged
State Revision only touches the flagged step — the rest of the trajectory is untouched
This is exactly the kind of contamination a pure environment-prediction model wouldn't catch
slides.title: Catching a false "done" before the agent commits to it

slides.body: AEWM adds a classification (and sometimes rewrite) step before every action, which costs latency and compute. Its gains are concentrated in long-horizon tasks where contamination has time to accumulate.
bullets: Every proposed step now costs an extra judge call — overhead that compounds on long runs
Action Judge is itself a trained component, calibrated on AEWM's own benchmark — not free with any backbone
Short, single-turn tasks have little contamination to catch, so the overhead buys less
slides.title: The judge isn't free, and short tasks barely need it

bullets: Predicting the effect of the agent's own next move catches a different class of error than predicting environment responses
Intervening before execution beats detecting the mistake after it's already logged
A three-way Critical/Exploratory/Noisy split lets the system intervene selectively, not on every single step
Released with its own Action-Judge benchmark dataset and Apache-2.0 code for reproducing the numbers
slides.title: Model what your actions will do to the task, not what the world will show you

questions.prompt: What does the paper mean by "task-state contamination"?
options: The training data containing duplicated examples
An agent's unsupported assumptions becoming accepted facts and partial progress being mistaken for completion
A GPU running out of memory mid-task
Two agents overwriting each other's files
questions.explanation: Task-state contamination is specifically about an agent's own reasoning corrupting its sense of task state over a long run — not a training-data or infrastructure issue.

questions.prompt: What three categories does Action Judge sort a proposed step into?
options: Fast, Slow, Expensive
Critical, Exploratory, Noisy
True, False, Unknown
Tool-call, Reasoning, Final-answer
questions.explanation: Action Judge classifies each proposed decision as Critical, Exploratory, or Noisy — only Noisy steps get rewritten by State Revision.

questions.prompt: What's a genuine limitation of AEWM's approach?
options: It only works on a single benchmark and backbone
It requires retraining the base LLM from scratch
It adds a judge-and-possibly-rewrite step before every action, so overhead is highest on short tasks with little contamination to catch
It cannot be combined with reinforcement fine-tuning
questions.explanation: The extra judge call before every proposed step is real overhead; the paper's gains concentrate on long-horizon tasks where contamination has time to accumulate, not short ones.

posts.title: Claude Code Mods: Rewriting the Agent From Inside
posts.subtitle: TypeScript functions that hook into Claude Code's own runtime events — no fork, no waiting for the next release.
posts.summary: Anthropic launched Claude Code mods on October 1, 2026 (tied to CLI v2.1.287): small TypeScript functions that hook into runtime events — tool calls, permission requests, UI rendering — to rewrite prompts, block or approve actions, redact output, or add custom UI. Mods ship inside existing plugins, stack in load order, and on Team/Enterprise plans a built-in sec-default mod loads first so user mods can't override org security policy.

bullets: Announced October 1, 2026 on the official Claude blog, tied to CLI version 2.1.287
Mods are small TypeScript functions that hook into Claude Code's own runtime events
Ship inside existing plugins — no separate install mechanism to learn
slides.title: Claude Code Can Now Be Rewritten From the Inside

slides.body: Before mods, changing how Claude Code behaves mid-run meant waiting for Anthropic to ship that exact feature, or working around the tool from the outside. Teams with specific permission policies, audit needs, or UI requirements had no hook point.
bullets: Prompts, tool calls, and permission prompts were fixed unless Anthropic shipped the change
No way to inject custom UI — panes, buttons, inputs — into the CLI or desktop app
Org-specific policies ("always double-confirm before touching prod") had nowhere to attach
slides.title: Official releases can't cover every team's workflow

slides.body: Claude Code now emits events for tool calls, permission requests, and UI rendering. A mod hooks into one of those events and runs before, after, or wrapped around it — rewriting prompts, blocking or retrying tool calls, approving or denying permissions, redacting secrets from output, or swapping in custom UI.
bullets: Mods are plain TypeScript functions — hand-written, or generated by asking Claude Code itself
Multiple mods stack in load order: the first-loaded mod sees the event first and the result last
Distributed through the same plugin marketplace and install flow Claude Code already has
slides.title: Hook into the event, run before/after/around it

headers: What a mod can do there
rows: Rewrite the prompt before it reaches the model
Block, rewrite, or retry the call
Auto-approve or auto-deny based on custom logic
Redact secrets before they're shown or logged
Add or replace panes, buttons, and inputs in CLI/desktop

slides.title: Five hook points, five different kinds of control

slides.body: A platform team writes a mod that hooks the tool-call event: any call touching a path under /prod/ is blocked unless it carries an extra, explicitly-typed confirmation string, and every approved call gets logged to the team's SIEM through the same hook. On a Team plan, this mod loads after the built-in sec-default mod, which already guarantees no mod — including this one — can silently override a permission denial.
bullets: The rule lives in one TypeScript function, not scattered across onboarding docs
It stacks under sec-default, which still has the final say on permission denials
Logging and the confirmation check both hook the same tool-call event, independently
slides.title: An org mod that enforces its own prod-safety rule

slides.body: Mods are arbitrary TypeScript executing inside your Claude Code session, which makes them powerful and a real supply-chain surface at the same time.
bullets: A mod has the same access as the session it's installed into — review untrusted ones like untrusted code
Load order matters: two mods hooking the same event can conflict rather than compose cleanly
On Team/Enterprise, sec-default loads first specifically so user-installed mods can't bypass org policy
Not a fit for a one-off tweak — simple preference changes are still better served by settings
slides.title: A mod runs with your session's own access — treat it like code, not config

bullets: Mods turn Claude Code into something teams can extend without waiting on Anthropic's roadmap
They ship as plugins, so discovery and distribution reuse the existing marketplace
Biggest win for org-specific guardrails today: audit logging, prod confirmations, permission policy
Still code with session-level access — vet a mod before installing it, especially anything touching permissions
slides.title: A customizable runtime, not a fork

posts.title: Event-Driven Architecture: Nobody Calls, Everyone Listens
posts.subtitle: Producers publish what happened; consumers decide for themselves whether they care.
posts.summary: Event-driven architecture inverts the usual dependency: producers publish an event and move on, with zero knowledge of who (if anyone) is listening. Consumers subscribe independently, so adding a new one never touches the producer's code. The tradeoff is real — harder debugging, no free ordering or delivery guarantees — but it's the pattern behind message queues, webhooks, and the hook systems agent tools increasingly use.

bullets: Core idea: producers emit events; consumers subscribe, without either side knowing the other exists
Powers message queues, webhooks, UI event handlers, and agent-tool hook systems alike
Contrast with request/response: the producer never blocks waiting for anyone's answer
slides.title: Systems That React Instead of Being Asked

slides.body: A request/response call means the caller must know exactly who to call and wait for the answer, breaking if that service moves or slows down. Polling avoids knowing the callee ahead of time, but trades that for wasted work — most polls come back with nothing new.
bullets: Direct calls couple services tightly: the caller breaks if the callee's address or API changes
Polling avoids that coupling but wastes cycles — most "anything new?" checks return no
Adding a third interested party (say, an audit log) means editing every existing caller's code
slides.title: Direct calls and polling both leak coupling

slides.body: An event-driven system inverts the dependency: a producer publishes "order placed" to a channel and moves on, with no knowledge of who's listening. Any number of consumers — billing, shipping, analytics — subscribe independently and react when the event arrives.
bullets: Producer and consumer are coupled only to the event's shape, never to each other directly
A new consumer can subscribe without changing a single line of the producer's code
Delivery can be synchronous (an in-process hook/callback) or asynchronous (a queue or event bus)
slides.title: Publish the fact, let interested parties subscribe

rows: Caller must know the callee's address
None — no call made, no cost
Caller knows what to ask, not when
Both sides only share an event schema
Idle until an event actually fires

slides.title: Three ways to find out something happened

slides.body: An "order placed" event fires once from the checkout service. Billing charges the card, shipping schedules a label, and marketing logs it for a win-back campaign — three subscribers added across three different product cycles, none of which touched checkout's code. The same pattern is why a Claude Code mod can hook a "tool_call" event without Claude Code's core ever importing that mod's code.
bullets: Each subscriber was added independently, long after the event itself shipped
Checkout's code has no idea billing, shipping, or marketing exist
The only shared contract is the shape of the "order placed" event
slides.title: One event, three subscribers, zero changes to checkout

slides.body: Event-driven systems trade immediate consistency and easy tracing for decoupling. If a downstream step absolutely must see an upstream result before continuing, forcing that through events adds indirection a direct call wouldn't have.
bullets: A failure surfaces far from its cause — producer and consumer are decoupled by design, so are their stack traces
No built-in guarantee of ordering or exactly-once delivery; the event bus has to provide that explicitly
Overkill for two components that will only ever talk to each other directly
Changing an event's schema breaks every subscriber silently, unless you version it
slides.title: The decoupling is real, and so is the debugging cost

bullets: Producers and consumers only ever agree on an event's shape — never on each other's existence
Adding a new consumer costs nothing on the producer's side — that's the entire point of the pattern
You pay for it in harder debugging and the need for explicit ordering/delivery guarantees
Shows up everywhere: message queues, webhooks, UI handlers, and now agent-tool hook systems
slides.title: The win is decoupling; the cost is traceability

questions.prompt: What's the core difference between event-driven architecture and direct request/response calls?
options: Event-driven systems are always faster at every single operation
In event-driven systems, the producer doesn't need to know who (if anyone) is listening; in request/response, the caller must know the callee and wait
Request/response can't be used over a network
There is no real difference, just different names
questions.explanation: The defining shift is that a producer publishes without knowing its consumers, versus a caller that must know exactly who to call and wait for a response.

questions.prompt: What's a genuine cost of adopting event-driven architecture?
options: It makes adding new consumers impossible
Debugging gets harder, and ordering/delivery guarantees aren't automatic — the event bus has to provide them
It requires every component to know about every other component
It eliminates the need for any schema design
questions.explanation: Decoupling producers from consumers means a failure's cause and effect are no longer adjacent in the code, and nothing guarantees ordering or exactly-once delivery unless the event bus is built to provide it.

questions.prompt: In the order-placed example, what had to change in checkout's code to add the email/marketing subscriber?
options: Checkout had to add a new function call to the marketing service
Nothing — the new subscriber just subscribes to the existing event
Checkout had to be rewritten to poll the marketing service
The event schema had to be redesigned from scratch
questions.explanation: That's the whole payoff of the pattern: a new consumer subscribes to an event that already exists, with zero changes required on the producer's side.

posts.title: CorpusMap: Giving Agentic Search a Memory of Entities
posts.subtitle: An offline entity graph lets search agents stop re-deriving the same document relationships on every query.
posts.summary: CorpusMap (arXiv:2609.37226, from KAIST/Microsoft researchers including Sung Ju Hwang) gives agentic search a navigation layer: an offline graph linking every document that mentions the same recurring entity. Across 7 models and 3 benchmarks, it improves evidence discovery and answer quality over raw agentic search while using fewer tokens, and beats four other navigation-layer designs.

slides.title: A Map of How Documents Relate, Built Once and Reused
bullets: Paper: "Follow the Entities: A Corpus Map for Agentic Search" (arXiv:2609.37226)
Authors: Soyeong Jeong, Sujay Kumar Jauhar, Sung Ju Hwang, Andrew Joohun Nam
Evaluated across 7 LLM backbones and 3 multi-document benchmarks

slides.title: A flat corpus forces every query to rediscover the same links
slides.body: Modern agentic search lets an LLM iteratively search a full corpus instead of reading a fixed top-k list. But when the corpus is just a pile of files, nothing tells the agent that two documents are about the same entity — so it has to re-establish that connection from scratch, every single query.
bullets: Relationships between documents aren't stored anywhere — the agent must infer them live
Complementary evidence spread across files gets missed when nothing links them
Re-deriving the same connections on every query burns extra search turns and tokens

slides.title: CorpusMap turns recurring entities into a graph, offline
slides.body: For every entity that recurs across the corpus, CorpusMap builds an Entity Page aggregating what's known about it plus links to every document that mentions it — forming an entity-document graph the agent can traverse at query time instead of rebuilding it.
bullets: Built once, offline, by resolving entity mentions across the whole corpus
Links are shared across every future query, not recomputed per-query
At inference, the agent jumps from an Entity Page straight to every linked document

slides.title: Better evidence, fewer tokens, across 7 models and 3 benchmarks
slides.body: Against raw agentic search over the same flat corpus, CorpusMap improved evidence discovery and final-answer quality while using fewer tokens on average, and outperformed four other navigation-layer designs tested in the paper.

slides.title: Tracing one drug across three differently-worded reports
slides.body: A biomedical corpus might mention a drug by its generic name in one trial report, its brand name in a second, and a side effect in a third — with nothing connecting them. Raw agentic search can read the first report, search again, and still miss the third. CorpusMap's entity resolution already merged the generic and brand names into one Entity Page linking all three documents, so a single lookup pulls the connected evidence together.
bullets: Entity resolution merges "drug X" and its brand name into one Entity Page
The agent jumps from that page to every linked document in one hop
Avoids the multi-turn search-and-miss cycle raw agentic search needs

slides.title: It only pays off when your corpus actually has recurring entities
slides.body: CorpusMap's gains come from entities that appear across many documents — people, products, organizations, named systems. A corpus of mostly one-off, self-contained documents gives the graph little to link, and the offline entity-resolution pass itself costs compute before the first query ever runs.
bullets: Upfront cost: entity resolution across the whole corpus runs once before any speedup
Weak entity overlap (mostly unique, one-off documents) limits the graph's value
It's a navigation layer on top of an existing agentic search loop, not a replacement for one

slides.title: Precompute the map; let the agent just walk it
bullets: Treat corpus navigation as a build-once offline asset, not something to re-derive every query
Entity resolution is the key moving part — link quality bounds graph quality
Drops into an existing agentic search loop as a navigation layer, not a new agent architecture
Best suited to corpora with recurring named entities: news, legal, biomedical, enterprise docs

questions.prompt: What problem does CorpusMap solve for agentic search?
options: It replaces the LLM with a dedicated retrieval model
It gives agents a pre-built map of how documents relate through shared entities
It compresses the corpus so it fits in the context window
It fine-tunes the agent directly on the corpus
questions.explanation: CorpusMap doesn't touch the model or compress documents — it precomputes entity-document relationships offline so agents don't have to rediscover them on every query.

questions.prompt: Why is CorpusMap built offline rather than at query time?
options: Because entities never repeat across documents in practice
So the relationship graph is computed once and reused across every future query instead of rebuilt each time
Because online computation is impossible for LLM agents
To avoid using any entity resolution at all
questions.explanation: Building the entity-document graph once, offline, means its links are shared across every future query rather than re-derived from scratch each time — that reuse is the whole efficiency win.

questions.prompt: According to the paper, what's a real limitation of CorpusMap's approach?
options: It requires retraining the base LLM
It only works with a single benchmark dataset
Its benefit depends on the corpus having recurring entities worth linking, and building the graph costs compute upfront
It cannot be combined with any existing agentic search system
questions.explanation: CorpusMap's gains come from linking entities that recur across documents; a corpus without much entity overlap gives the graph little to work with, and the offline build itself is an upfront cost.

references.title: Follow the Entities: A Corpus Map for Agentic Search (arXiv:2609.37226)

posts.title: SynthID Bio: Watermarking AI-Designed Proteins
posts.subtitle: Google DeepMind hides a detectable signature in both a protein's sequence and its 3D structure — without changing how it works.
posts.summary: On Sept 30, 2026, Google DeepMind introduced SynthID Bio, extending its SynthID watermarking family into biology. It embeds a detectable signature into both an AI-designed protein's amino acid sequence and its predicted 3D structure, and wet-lab tests across three target proteins showed watermarked designs matched unwatermarked ones in hit rate and binding affinity.

slides.title: An Invisible Signature Inside AI-Designed Proteins
bullets: Announced by Google DeepMind, September 30, 2026
Extends the SynthID family (already used for text and images) into biology
Open-sourced for biosecurity partners, aimed at DNA synthesis screening

slides.title: AI can design proteins that match nothing in a threat database
slides.body: DNA synthesis providers screen orders against databases of known hazards before manufacturing a sequence. But AI-designed proteins can look nothing like any known pathogen or toxin — so an unfamiliar sequence can't be safely assumed harmless, and resolving that ambiguity by hand is slow enough to stall legitimate research.
bullets: Screening databases are built around known threats, not novel AI-generated sequences
An unfamiliar sequence is ambiguous: could be a harmless design or something concerning
Manual review to resolve that ambiguity can stall legitimate orders

slides.title: Two watermarks: one in the sequence, one in the structure
slides.body: For amino acid sequences, SynthID Bio uses a secret key to subtly bias which amino acid gets suggested at each position, while ProteinMPNN rejects any suggestion that would break the protein's function. For predicted 3D structures, it fine-tunes a small part of AlphaFold 3's diffusion network so the watermark is baked directly into the output atomic coordinates.
bullets: Sequence watermark: key-guided amino acid bias, checked by ProteinMPNN so function isn't broken
Structure watermark: a fine-tuned slice of AlphaFold 3's diffusion network nudges atomic coordinates
Detection: software rescans with the same key and measures how often the key-suggested amino acids appear
The key is shared only with trusted partners, like DNA synthesis providers — never published

slides.title: Wet-lab tested on three real target proteins
slides.body: In lab testing, watermarked designs matched the hit rate, binding affinity, and natural sequence diversity of unwatermarked versions — the watermark didn't change how the proteins worked.

slides.title: A synthesis order that used to need a human to resolve
slides.body: A biotech lab submits a DNA order for an AI-designed binder to VEGF-A that looks nothing like any natural sequence. Today, a screening provider would flag that for manual review. With the detection key, the same provider's software rescans the sequence, finds the embedded watermark, and confirms it came from a known, trusted AI design pipeline — no manual escalation needed.
bullets: Before: unfamiliar sequence triggers a slow manual safety review
After: a key-based rescan confirms provenance in software, automatically

slides.title: The watermark only works if the key stays secret and partners adopt it
slides.body: SynthID Bio's security model depends on the detection key never leaking and on synthesis providers actually wiring the check into their screening pipeline. It also can't watermark sequences from AI tools that don't integrate it, so it doesn't solve the problem for designs made outside the SynthID ecosystem.
bullets: Protection depends on the key staying secret — leak it, and the mark can be forged or stripped
Only covers proteins from tools that integrate SynthID Bio; non-adopting tools stay unmarked
Adoption by DNA synthesis providers is voluntary, not yet a universal screening requirement

slides.title: A watermark that survives synthesis and folding intact
bullets: First demonstration that a biological watermark survives wet-lab synthesis and folding without changing function
Extends the SynthID approach, already used for text and images, into biological design
Positioned as a biosecurity tool for synthesis screening and database integrity, not a design feature
Real-world impact depends on adoption by synthesis providers and other AI protein-design tools

questions.prompt: What does SynthID Bio embed a watermark into?
options: The lab's ordering software only
The amino acid sequence and the predicted 3D structure of a designed protein
The DNA synthesis machine's firmware
A visible label printed on the lab sample
questions.explanation: SynthID Bio watermarks both the sequence (via key-guided amino acid choices) and the predicted 3D structure (via a fine-tuned AlphaFold 3 diffusion network).

questions.prompt: How does SynthID Bio watermark predicted 3D structures without breaking their function?
options: By randomly perturbing atom positions
By fine-tuning a small part of AlphaFold 3's diffusion network to nudge atomic coordinates
By adding a visible tag to the output file's metadata
By lowering the structure's resolution
questions.explanation: The structure watermark comes from fine-tuning a slice of AlphaFold 3's diffusion network, so the signal lives in the model's output coordinates rather than being bolted on afterward.

questions.prompt: What's a real limitation of this approach?
options: It only works on RNA, not proteins
Its protection depends on the secret key staying secret and on synthesis providers adopting the check
It makes every watermarked protein 50% less stable
It requires discarding AlphaFold entirely
questions.explanation: SynthID Bio's security model is only as strong as key secrecy and provider adoption — it can't help with sequences from tools that don't integrate it, or if the key leaks.

posts.title: DPO: Skipping the Reward Model in RLHF
posts.subtitle: Direct Preference Optimization turns a three-stage RLHF pipeline into one classification-style loss on preference pairs.
posts.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) replaces classic RLHF's separate reward model and unstable PPO loop with a single, closed-form loss computed directly on preference pairs. It trains like supervised fine-tuning, but it trades away the reusable reward model that RLHF leaves behind.

slides.title: Turning Human Preferences Directly Into a Training Loss
bullets: Introduced by Rafailov et al. (Stanford), 2023 — arXiv:2305.18290
Skips the reward model and PPO loop that classic RLHF needs
Now a common default alignment step behind many open-weight chat models

slides.title: Classic RLHF is a three-stage pipeline that's hard to get right
slides.body: To align a model with human preferences, RLHF first trains a separate reward model on comparison data, then runs reinforcement learning — typically PPO — against that reward model. The RL stage is notoriously unstable, needs careful tuning, and requires sampling from the live policy during training.
bullets: Stage 1: collect human preference pairs (response A preferred over response B)
Stage 2: train a separate reward model to score any response
Stage 3: run PPO against that reward model, tuning a KL penalty to avoid collapse

slides.title: DPO folds the reward model into the policy itself
slides.body: DPO's key move: the optimal RLHF policy has a closed-form relationship to the reward function. Substituting that relationship back into the reward-modeling loss removes the reward model entirely, leaving a simple classification loss computed directly on the policy's log-probabilities for the preferred vs. dispreferred response.
bullets: Loss = a sigmoid of the log-probability ratio between chosen and rejected responses, scaled by β
β controls how far the new policy is allowed to drift from the frozen reference model
No reward model, no PPO sampling loop — training looks like standard supervised fine-tuning

slides.title: Same goal, very different training pipeline
slides.body: Both methods optimize a policy toward human preferences, but DPO removes two of RLHF's moving parts: the standalone reward model and the online RL sampling loop.

rows: Trains like a standard supervised loss
Policy via RL against a learned reward

slides.title: Picking between two draft replies
slides.body: Say a dataset has one prompt with two candidate replies, and human raters preferred reply A over reply B. DPO's loss increases the model's log-probability of generating A — relative to the frozen reference model — and decreases it for B, in a single gradient step, with no reward model ever scoring either reply.
bullets: Input: one prompt, one preferred reply, one rejected reply
DPO directly increases P(preferred) and decreases P(rejected), relative to the reference model
β = 0.1 is a common default — it keeps the updated policy close enough to the reference to avoid degenerate outputs that just game the preference signal

slides.title: DPO trades flexibility for simplicity
slides.body: Because DPO never trains an explicit reward model, there's no reusable scoring function left over for things like best-of-n reranking at inference time. DPO is also entirely dependent on preference-pair quality — there's no independent reward model to regularize or inspect if the labels are noisy.
bullets: No standalone reward model left over for reranking or filtering outside of training
Entirely dependent on preference-pair quality; noisy labels directly corrupt the policy
Still requires keeping a frozen reference model in memory during training for the implicit KL term

slides.title: One loss, no reward model, no RL loop
bullets: DPO collapses RLHF's reward-model-then-PPO pipeline into one direct classification-style loss
β is the main knob: higher trusts the preference data more, lower stays closer to the reference model
Big practical win: no reward model to maintain, no unstable RL sampling loop to tune
Still only as good as the preference data — noisy preferences in, degraded alignment out

questions.prompt: What does DPO eliminate compared to classic RLHF with PPO?
options: The need for any human preference data
The separate reward model and the online RL sampling loop
The frozen reference model
The use of log-probabilities during training
questions.explanation: DPO substitutes the closed-form relationship between the optimal policy and the reward directly into the loss, so there's no reward model to train and no PPO rollouts to sample.

questions.prompt: In DPO's loss, what does the β parameter control?
options: The learning rate schedule
How much data is used per training batch
How far the updated policy is allowed to drift from the frozen reference model
The number of preference pairs required
questions.explanation: β scales the log-probability ratio in DPO's loss, playing a role similar to the KL penalty in RLHF — higher β trusts the preference labels more, lower β stays closer to the reference model.

questions.prompt: What's a real limitation of DPO compared to RLHF with an explicit reward model?
options: DPO can't use human preference data at all
DPO leaves no standalone reward model you could reuse later, e.g. for reranking
DPO always requires more GPUs than PPO
DPO can only be applied to vision models
questions.explanation: Because DPO folds the reward signal directly into the policy update, there's no separate scoring model left over afterward — a real tradeoff against RLHF, where the reward model remains usable independently.
